analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2003 tax cuts on investment dividends and capital gains permanent, ending their scheduled expiration.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote; the dividend and capital gains cuts it would have made permanent instead ran through 2008 and were separately extended through 2010 before expiring, and were permanently extended for most taxpayers in 2012.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2003 Congress cut the top tax rate on dividends to 15% and lowered the capital gains rate, but wrote the cuts to expire in 2008. This bill would repeal the expiration date, making the lower rates permanent. Lower rates on dividends and capital gains overwhelmingly benefit households with large investment portfolios, and making them permanent would lock in the lost federal revenue indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with substantial investment income — shareholders and upper-income taxpayers who receive dividends and realize capital gains — get a permanent lock-in of the lower 15% rates. The financial services industry also benefits from keeping the favorable treatment of investment returns.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sunset in Section 303 of the Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2003, making the reduced dividend and capital gains tax rates permanent rather than letting them expire.
In 2003, the top tax rate on dividends was cut to 15% and the capital gains rate was reduced, with both scheduled to revert to higher rates in 2008.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a whole, since making the investment tax cuts permanent deepens the federal deficit and shifts more of the tax burden toward wage earners; in practice the cost is concentrated on future budgets, funded by borrowing or by higher taxes on other income.

drawbacks.text: The benefits are heavily concentrated: households with investment portfolios, which skew toward the top of the income distribution, receive nearly all of the savings, while wage earners gain little or nothing.
Making the cuts permanent removes the built-in expiration that gave Congress a chance to reassess; the lost revenue would continue indefinitely, adding to federal deficits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows to a narrow group — investors with large portfolios — at the cost of indefinitely forgoing federal revenue that would otherwise revert in 2008. As a matter of design, it entrenches a tax preference for wealth over work with no offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2004 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 without any further action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Jon Kyl on June 3, 2004 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was taken — the bill never received a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

The same policy — extending the dividend and capital gains cuts — was pursued through other vehicles during the period and the cuts were ultimately extended through 2010 and later made permanent for most taxpayers under the 2012 American Taxpayer Relief Act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one directly, because the bill never became law; but the underlying 2003 cuts were preserved through extensions by later Congresses, so investors benefited from the rates lasting longer than the original 2008 expiration — just not through this bill's mechanism of making them permanent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investors, via later extensions of the cuts

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the dividend and capital gains tax cuts permanent; joined by three Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican support (sponsor plus 3 Republican cosponsors); it never advanced to a vote, so no opposition voting record exists.

industries.note: Permanent lower rates on dividends and capital gains sustain a tax preference for investment income over wages, benefiting the industry's clients and incentive structures. Ordinary workers gain nothing and bear the deferred fiscal cost.
Top-rate taxpayers with large portfolios capture nearly all of the benefit of permanent lower rates.
